content: Many women with epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) develop resistance to standard chemotherapy drugs. Angiogenesis inhibitors, which block the formation of new blood vessels necessary for tumor growth, aim to control cancer progression by cutting off the blood supply to tumor nodules. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and toxicities of angiogenesis inhibitors in the treatment of EOC. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase databases, covering studies from 1990 to September 30, 2022. Additional information was obtained from clinical trial registries and direct communication with investigators of completed and ongoing trials. The inclusion criteria focused on RCTs comparing angiogenesis inhibitors with standard chemotherapy, other anti-cancer treatments, other angiogenesis inhibitors (with or without additional treatments), or placebo/no treatment in a maintenance setting for women with EOC. The analysis included 50 studies with a total of 14,836 participants. These studies were divided into those involving newly-diagnosed EOC (13 studies) and recurrent EOC (37 studies). Among the recurrent EOC studies, nine focused on platinum-sensitive disease, 19 on platinum-resistant disease, and nine on mixed or unclear platinum sensitivity. Newly-Diagnosed EOC: 1. Bevacizumab (a monoclonal antibody targeting VEGF): When combined with chemotherapy and continued as maintenance, bevacizumab likely results in little to no difference in overall survival (OS) compared to chemotherapy alone (HR 0.97; moderate-certainty evidence). Progression-free survival (PFS) data is very uncertain (HR 0.82; very low-certainty evidence). The combination slightly reduces global quality of life (QoL) (MD -6.4; high-certainty evidence). It likely increases the risk of severe adverse events (grade ≥ 3) (RR 1.16; moderate-certainty evidence) and may result in a significant increase in hypertension (grade ≥ 2) (RR 4.27; low-certainty evidence). 2. Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs) targeting VEGF receptors: When combined with chemotherapy and continued as maintenance, TKIs likely result in little to no difference in OS (HR 0.99; moderate-certainty evidence). They likely provide a slight improvement in PFS (HR 0.88; moderate-certainty evidence). QoL is slightly reduced (MD -1.86; moderate-certainty evidence). The combination slightly increases the risk of severe adverse events (grade ≥ 3) (RR 1.31; moderate-certainty evidence) and may result in a significant increase in hypertension (grade ≥ 3) (RR 6.49; low-certainty evidence). Recurrent EOC (Platinum-Sensitive): 1. Bevacizumab: When combined with chemotherapy and continued as maintenance, bevacizumab likely results in little to no difference in OS (HR 0.90; moderate-certainty evidence). It likely improves PFS (HR 0.56; moderate-certainty evidence). QoL may show little to no difference (MD 0.8; low-certainty evidence). The combination slightly increases the rate of severe adverse events (grade ≥ 3) (RR 1.11; high-certainty evidence). Hypertension (grade ≥ 3) is more common with bevacizumab (RR 5.82). 2. TKIs: When combined with chemotherapy, TKIs may result in little to no difference in OS (HR 0.86; low-certainty evidence). They likely improve PFS (HR 0.56; moderate-certainty evidence). QoL may show little to no difference (MD 6.1; low-certainty evidence). Hypertension (grade ≥ 3) is more common with TKIs (RR 3.32). Recurrent EOC (Platinum-Resistant): 1. Bevacizumab: When combined with chemotherapy and continued as maintenance, bevacizumab improves OS (HR 0.73; high-certainty evidence). It likely results in a significant improvement in PFS (HR 0.49; moderate-certainty evidence). The combination may result in a significant increase in hypertension (grade ≥ 2) (RR 3.11; low-certainty evidence). The rate of bowel fistula or perforation (grade ≥ 2) may be slightly higher with bevacizumab (RR 6.89; very low-certainty evidence). 2. TKIs: When combined with chemotherapy, TKIs likely result in little to no difference in OS (HR 0.85; moderate-certainty evidence). They may increase PFS (HR 0.70; low-certainty evidence). QoL may show little to no meaningful difference (MD ranged from -0.19 to -3.40). The combination slightly increases the rate of severe adverse events (grade ≥ 3) (RR 1.23; high-certainty evidence). The effect on bowel fistula or perforation rates is uncertain (RR 2.74; very low-certainty evidence). Authors' Conclusions: Bevacizumab likely improves both OS and PFS in platinum-resistant relapsed EOC. In platinum-sensitive relapsed disease, both bevacizumab and TKIs probably improve PFS, but their impact on OS remains uncertain. For newly-diagnosed EOC, the effects on OS and PFS are less clear, with a noted decrease in QoL and an increase in adverse events. Overall, while there appears to be a role for anti-angiogenesis treatments, the additional treatment burden and economic costs of maintenance therapies necessitate careful consideration of their benefits and risks.
